children: The Head - People & Culture on why plants running automation, AI, analytics and robotics at scale must present themselves as technology-enabled innovators, and what young engineers look for beyond a salary

As India’s steel industry expands towards 300 million tonnes of capacity, the companies that line its furnaces must grow their people as fast as their customers grow their output. KT Rao, Head - People & Culture, RHI Magnesita India, explains why capability matters more than headcount, how safety must become a daily habit for permanent and contract workers alike, and why heavy industry must present itself as a technology career to win the next generation of engineers.
As Indian steelmakers expand towards 300 million tonnes of capacity, how should a refractories supplier build the technical and field-service talent to keep pace?

As India’s steel industry expands towards 300 million tonnes of capacity, refractories companies must focus on building specialised technical and field-service capabilities, not just increasing headcount. The future workforce will need deeper expertise in applications, process optimisation, and digital tools that help customers improve performance and efficiency. At RHI Magnesita, we view talent development as a strategic investment through continuous learning, global knowledge sharing, and strong on-site technical support, enabling us to partner effectively with customers in their growth journey.
Leading people strategy across India, West Asia and Africa, how do you keep one culture while workplace expectations differ so much between regions?

At RHI Magnesita, we maintain one global culture built on common values, leadership principles, and a shared purpose. At the same time, we recognise that employee expectations vary across regions, including India. The key is balancing global consistency with local relevance. We achieve this through strong leadership visibility, open communication, and regular employee engagement, ensuring people feel connected to the same organisation while addressing local needs and realities
In high-temperature, heavy-industry settings, what makes a safety culture work in practice, on the shop floor and among contract workers?

In a heavy-industry environment like ours, safety culture works only when it becomes a daily habit rather than a compliance requirement. It starts with visible leadership commitment, regular safety conversations on the shop floor, and empowering people to stop unsafe work without fear. Equally important is ensuring that the same safety standards apply to everyone, irrespective of whether they are permanent employees, contract workers, or leaders across shop floors or corporate offices. Through consistent training, supervision, accountability, and open reporting, we create a culture where safety is a shared responsibility and production goals are never achieved at the cost of people’s well-being.
As steel and cement customers move towards lower-carbon production, which new skills will a refractories business need, and how should HR build them?

As steel and cement producers accelerate their decarbonisation journey, the refractories industry will need new capabilities beyond traditional manufacturing expertise. Skills in sustainability, carbon accounting, circular economy practices, advanced materials, digitalisation, and data-driven process optimisation will become increasingly important.

For HR, the focus should be on building these capabilities through a combination of targeted hiring, upskilling existing talent, and creating cross-functional learning opportunities with customers and technology teams. The biggest opportunity lies in reskilling our current workforce, combining their deep industry knowledge with new sustainability and digital competencies. This will enable us to remain a strategic partner to customers as they transition to lower-carbon production.
How can core industrial companies attract and keep young engineers and technicians who often look first at technology careers?

Industrial companies need to stop positioning themselves as traditional manufacturing employers and start showcasing themselves as technology-enabled innovators. Today's plants use automation, AI, analytics, robotics, and digital manufacturing at scale, which offers exciting opportunities for young engineers. To attract and retain talent, organisations must combine cutting-edge technology exposure with accelerated career growth, continuous learning, meaningful work, and strong leadership. Young professionals are looking for purpose, development, and impact. Companies that provide these, along with modern workplace experiences and opportunities to innovate, will remain employers of choice for the next generation of engineers and technicians.
Heavy industry depends on deep hands-on know-how. How should companies capture and pass on that experience as digital tools arrive and the workforce changes?

Heavy industry has always relied on deep hands-on expertise built over decades. As digital tools and AI become more prevalent, the priority is not to replace that experience, but to capture, preserve, and scale it. Companies need to systematically document critical know-how through digital knowledge platforms, mentorship programmes, video-based learning, and communities of practice. The most successful organisations will combine the wisdom of experienced employees with the speed and analytical power of modern technology, ensuring valuable knowledge is transferred seamlessly to the next generation.
